Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Rylan Barton. The FAA has declared a nationwide
ground stop. Officials have said there's no indication of a threat to the U.S. and that
this appears to be a technical failing. NPR's Ava Berger is at Reagan National Airport outside
Washington, D.C. I'm sitting on the ground with a lot of other people here tonight,
and a lot of people are telling me they're still in the dark. They don't know what's happening.
They haven't heard a lot from their airline. I was sitting with someone when they got a
notification that their flight was delayed an hour. But despite no one really knowing
what's going on at this time, it's pretty calm here. People have told me they're used to being
delayed and they're going to wait it out. Although I talked to some people who did not want to check
their bags quite yet to avoid that headache of losing their bags. And as I'm looking at this
flight board, I'm seeing more and more red, more flights getting canceled. And we do know that
about 2,000 flights have been canceled so far. NPR's Ava Berger reporting. Democrats say they
have a mandate to deliver change when they take control of Congress next year. But there are
divides over how far that change should go and who should lead it. As NPR's Elena Moore reports,
that debate is playing out in the Senate where Minority Leader Chuck Schumer now faces a
challenge from fellow Democrat Chris Van Hollen for the top job next year. Van Hollen has represented
Maryland in the Senate since 2017 and leans more progressive. He announced his intention to
challenge Schumer Thursday night and says the midterm showed how much voters want Democrats
to reject the status quo. It comes as Schumer has faced questions about his leadership in
recent years and a handful of incoming soon-to-be senators have declined to support him. But despite
that, Van Hollen acknowledges he's an underdog in this race and Schumer has said he has the needed
votes to win. The race will ultimately be decided in early December when the caucus votes. Elena Moore
and Pierre News. An advocacy group for parents has written to two state attorneys general to
investigate open A.I. for allegedly failing to protect children from the harms posed by chat
G.P.T. NPR's Ritu Chatterjee reports the company is already facing multiple lawsuits from parents
who say their kids have been harmed by the chatbot. More than 60 parents of children harmed by tech
platforms have signed the letter to attorneys general Rob Bonta of California and Kathy Jennings
of Delaware. Among those parents are Maria and Matt Raine, parents of Adam Raine, a 16-year-old
who died by suicide after prolonged interactions with chat G.P.T. Juliana Arnold is a founding
member of the advocacy group Parents Rise, which drafted the letter. They've been releasing
products that are not safe. Kids have died. People are being harmed. Arnold and others say they're
asking the states to investigate open A.I.'s governance structure to learn what's preventing
the company from prioritizing safety over profits. Bonta is already probing recent cybersecurity
incidents at open A.I. Ritu Chatterjee, NPR News. U.S. stocks fell today. The S&P 500 fell four
tenths of a percent, but closed with a weekly gain of two and a half percent. This is NPR News.
U.S. and U.K. defense officials say unauthorized drone activity prompted a security response at an
American base in Britain, but the situation has been resolved. Three U.S. bases in the U.K. have
been affected by threats in recent weeks. It's been about a year since New Mexico became the
first state to offer free child care to every eligible family regardless of income. NPR's
Julie Deppenbrock reports demand is outpacing capacity. Ready? We're going to march outside.
Ready? One, two, three. March. March. Across the country, there is a shortage of child care
workers. Olga Grace operates out of her home in Las Cruces, New Mexico. She's been a child care
provider for more than two decades. The pay is really not, it doesn't go with the amount of work
that we put into what we do, right? It's not valued enough. According to the Center for American
Progress, nearly half of all children in the U.S. live in a licensed child care desert where demand
outpaces availability. Still, the idea of free universal child care is taking hold around the
country as state and local leaders watch and try to learn from New Mexico's ambitious experiment.
Julie Deppenbrock, NPR News. The U.S. Mint is printing $1 coins for each state over the next
six years, and this week Washington Governor Bob Ferguson announced theirs will feature
guitar legend Jimi Hendrix. It's slated to be released in 2029. Starting in 2019, the Mint
launched a $1 coin series celebrating innovation. 32 state coins have been produced so far.
California's shows Steve Jobs, Minnesota's highlights the invention of mobile refrigeration.
This is NPR News from Washington. This message comes from Rosetta Stone. Rosetta Stone is
designed to make language learning intuitive. It mimics how people naturally acquire speech as
children, helping users read, write, and think in a second language. More at RosettaStone.com.
